the effects of solar radiation on the mass balance of glaciers in the European Alps.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
solar radiation is a key driver of glacier melt in the European Alps, and that the 1940‐1950s period was the warmest and sunniest period in the last century.
the glacier melt of the 1940’s was due to enhanced solar irradiance, and the glacier melt of recent decades was due to increased air temperature.
solar dimming and brighting has a strong impact on the mass balance of glaciers in the European Alps.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the glacier melt in the European Alps in the 194os was stronger than today in spite of higher air temperature.
the 1940’s was a time of enhanced solar radiation and strong glacier melt, whereas the 1970s and 1980s were characterized by a reduced solar radiation input and advancing glaciers.
the 1940's was an exceptional period for the glaciers in the European Alps.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the impact of changes in global solar radiation on glaciers can be as important as that of air temperature.
solar radiation has a strong effect on glacier mass balance and that this effect is not only limited to the ablation season, but also affects snow accumulation and winter mass balance.
the impact of global dimming on glacier melt is not only limited to the 1950–1980 period but also extends to the 1940–1960 period.
